title: The Town Hall Is Broken and Leaders Know It
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Ghassan Karian argues that the all-hands meeting has become a ritual that produces the appearance of agreement while the real conversation moves to the car park and the private chat group. Drawing on the 2026 IC Index from Ipsos Karian and Box, he shows that trust has fallen and that leaders are far more confident than their employees that messaging is landing and the CEO is honest. He adds that line managers, not senior leaders, are the most trusted source of information on job security and team direction, so treating them as message carriers wastes the organisation's best trust asset. Extra channels such as intranet posts, CEO video blogs and slow pulse surveys are dismissed as broadcast dressed up as dialogue. Real two-way communication needs small groups, psychological safety and leaders willing to hear and act on awkward questions, as in Aviva's employee takeovers of internal communications. His conclusion is that the fix is not a better strategy but leaders who say difficult things clearly and admit what they do not know.
points: Town halls generate the appearance of alignment while employees quietly disbelieve what they are told, and the survey data shows leaders consistently overestimate how well their message lands.
Line managers are the most credible channel in most organisations, so communication plans should equip them to run conversations rather than just relay announcements.
Adding intranet articles, CEO video blogs and delayed pulse surveys does not fix the problem because these are broadcast tools posing as dialogue.
Genuine two-way communication needs small groups, psychological safety and visible action on hard questions, and handing the microphone to frontline staff is one workable model.
The remedy is candour: acknowledge what you do not know and treat people as capable of handling the truth.
quotes: The gap between what organisations communicate and what employees actually believe is one of the most thoroughly documented and least acted-upon problems in organisational life. It has its own data, its own literature and it is getting worse.

The leaders designing the communications believe, with reasonable confidence, that their messaging is landing, believed and trusted. The people receiving it are, in significant numbers, not buying it.

The result is a communication system that is technically functioning (messages are being sent, received, and politely acknowledged) while culturally failing. The town hall happens but nothing changes.

If line managers are the most credible communication channel in most organisations, then the communication strategy that ignores them (that treats them as message carriers rather than conversation facilitators) is not just inefficient. It is actively undermining the most valuable trust asset the organisation has.

The standard response to the town hall’s inadequacy is to add more channels: the intranet article that nobody reads, the CEO video blog with a comment section that nobody uses, the pulse survey whose results are shared in aggregate six weeks later with no visible action. These are the town hall’s digital cousins; broadcast mechanisms dressed up as dialogue.

Genuine two-way communication (the kind that rebuilds trust rather than merely performing it) has structural requirements that most organisations find uncomfortable. It requires small groups, not large ones. It requires leaders who are genuinely willing to hear difficult things and be seen to act on them.

The solution is not a better communications strategy. It is leaders who are willing to say difficult things clearly, to acknowledge what they don’t know, and to treat the people they lead as capable of handling the truth.
That sounds obvious. It is also, in most organisations, revolutionary. Which tells you something about how low the bar has been set.
